bib.title: LILA: A Unified Benchmark for Mathematical Reasoning

read.skipped: Reference list and the tail of Table 21 (per-dataset scores) skimmed only.

question: Can a single unified benchmark of math reasoning tasks, with program solutions, OOD and robustness splits, measure and improve general mathematical reasoning?
hypothesis: Multi-task training on diverse math datasets with program annotations improves in-distribution and OOD performance over single-task models.
contributions: LILA benchmark: 20 datasets extended with Python programs and instructions, 23 tasks over 4 dimensions, plus OOD and robustness evaluation
Analysis: multitasking helps, program synthesis beats answer prediction, few-shot Codex strongest

method.summary: Unify 20 math datasets into one format (question, answer, Python programs, instruction), define 23 tasks across 4 categories, split IID/OOD/ROBUST, then fine-tune GPT-Neo-2.7B single- and multi-task and few-shot prompt GPT-3 and Codex.
method.task: mathematical reasoning (program synthesis vs direct answer)

datasets.name: LILA (44 sub-datasets from 20 sources)
datasets.split: 70% train / 10% dev / 20% test IID; plus LILA-OOD and LILA-ROBUST
datasets.source: 20 existing math datasets (Table 22) extended with Python programs and instructions; github.com/allenai/Lila
datasets.preprocessing: DSL-to-Python rules, pattern matching, regenerated DeepMind/AMPS with programs, expert annotation; some datasets (e.g. AMPS) downsampled by random selection

datasets.name: LILA-OOD
datasets.size: not stated as one total (per-task held-out datasets; see Tables 15-18)
datasets.source: Datasets randomly assigned to OOD per task

datasets.name: LILA-ROBUST
datasets.size: 20 questions per constituent dataset x 9 templates

models.name: GPT-Neo-2.7B single-task (Neo-A, Neo-P)
models.init_from: GPT-Neo pretrained on the Pile (natural language and code)

other.outputs: trained to output both final answer and Python program

training.objective: inferred: causal LM fine-tuning to emit answer and Python program given question

other.note: Section 4 'Compute' heading in the text gives no numbers; no hyperparameters stated in the paper

inference.samples: one run; GPT-3 and Codex on 100 uniformly distributed examples per task
inference.prompting: few-shot with random input-output examples from same dataset (IID) or other datasets of the same task (OOD); 0, 1, 3, max examples; with or without task instruction

other.program_execution: model output executed in Python interpreter; roughly 10% Neo-Multi IID programs fail to execute

metrics.name: F1
metrics.definition: soft exact match with partial credit for common words, between model answer (or executed program output) and gold answer

eval.protocol: Evaluation on program output rather than program text; IID, OOD and ROBUST sets; no seeds or significance tests reported

results.claim: Multi-task Neo-Multi-P beats single-task Neo-P on in-distribution average F1 (0.480 vs 0.394).
results.setup: LILA IID test split (20% per task), GPT-Neo-2.7B fine-tuned, program-synthesis output, 23 tasks averaged
results.quote: Neo-Multi achieves better average in-domain performance than the 23 individual per-task models (0.480 vs. 0.394 average score)

results.claim: Multi-task training raises OOD average F1 from 0.238 to 0.448 for program synthesis.
results.setup: LILA-OOD, GPT-Neo-2.7B program output, Neo-Multi-P vs Neo-P
results.note: Table 4 prints Neo-P IID 0.394 / OOD 0.263 as dimension averages, while Table 3 prints Neo-P OOD average 0.238; the two tables aggregate differently.
results.quote: multi-task training substantially improves out-of-domain generalization (0.448 vs. 0.238)

results.claim: Abstract: average relative improvement of multi-task over single-task models is 21.83% F1.
results.setup: LILA, multi-task GPT-Neo-2.7B vs single-task models
results.quote: average relative improvement of 21.83% F1 score vs. single-task models

results.claim: Best model (few-shot Codex, program synthesis) scores only 60.40% F1 on LILA.
results.setup: Codex code-davinci-002, few-shot (max examples), computed on 100 uniformly distributed examples per task
results.note: Table 3 prints the Codex IID average as 0.604; the 60.40% in abstract/conclusion matches it.
results.quote: while the best performing model only obtains 60.40%

results.claim: Program synthesis roughly doubles multi-task F1 over direct answer prediction (0.480 vs 0.252).
results.setup: LILA IID, Neo-Multi-P vs Neo-Multi-A, GPT-Neo-2.7B
results.quote: multi-task program synthesis (Neo-Multi-P) has an average score of 0.480 while multi-task answer prediction (Neo-Multi-A) scores 0.252

results.claim: Few-shot Codex IID/OOD average F1: 0.604 IID, 0.586 OOD.
results.setup: LILA Table 3 average row, Codex 175B few-shot, 100 examples per task
results.table: Table 3, row Average score, columns Codex IID and OOD

results.claim: Single-task GPT-Neo-2.7B program output shows a large IID to OOD drop (0.394 to 0.238), whereas Neo-Multi-P drops less (0.480 to 0.448).
results.setup: LILA Table 3 average row, Neo-P OOD
results.table: Table 3, row Average score, column Neo-P OOD

results.claim: About 10% of Neo-Multi IID programs fail to execute; 86% of those are SyntaxErrors.
results.quote: Roughly 10% of Neo-Multi’s IID programs fail to execute. 86% of these are SyntaxErrors

results.claim: Instructions help only zero-shot for GPT-3: average IID 0.148 w/o vs 0.156 w/ instruction; few-shot(3) 0.396 vs 0.390.
results.setup: GPT-3 IID, zero-shot and 3-shot, with and without task instructions
results.table: Table 6, row Average, columns Zero-shot w/ Inst

results.claim: Neo-Multi is a better starting point for fine-tuning: T5-3B-style direct QA improves from 30.1% to 37.6% F1.
results.setup: Fine-tuning on held-out LILA-OOD data, direct answer, starting from Neo-Multi vs vanilla GPT-Neo-2.7B
results.note: Text mentions T5-3B but Table 5 compares Neo and Multi (GPT-Neo-2.7B); Table 5 100% row answer F1 is 28.4 vs 32.3, which does not match 30.1/37.6. Inconsistent in the paper.
results.quote: we see an almost 8% absolute improvement in F1 (30.1% to 37.6%)

results.claim: LILA has 133,815 questions and 358,769 programs across 23 tasks, 44 datasets.
IID split is a random 70/10/20 train/dev/test partition within each task.
results.quote: we randomly partition the data in each task into training (70%), development (10%) and test (20%) sets

results.claim: LILA-ROBUST uses 20 sampled questions per constituent dataset and 9 perturbation templates (3 from SVAMP, 6 new) rewritten by MTurk workers.
results.setup: Crowdsourced via AMT, $3 per HIT, workers >98% acceptance and >1000 HITs
results.quote: we define a total of 9 templates for such question perturbations: 3 from Patel et al. (2021) and 6 of our own

results.claim: Multi-task model showed no degradation on perturbed IID test examples.
results.quote: we did not find any degradation in performance when testing on perturbed IID test examples

results.claim: The OOD split assigns whole datasets of a task to IID or OOD at random; tasks with a single dataset get no OOD set.
results.quote: randomly assigning the datasets for each task into IID and an OOD sets

results.claim: Few-shot Codex scores under 0.5 F1 on geometry, number theory, advanced math, complex language, computer science, science formulas, real-world knowledge.
results.quote: Codex obtains less that 0.5 F1 on several tasks

results.claim: GPT-3 and Codex numbers use only 100 uniformly distributed examples per task; fine-tuned on full test set.
results.quote: GPT-3 and Codex performance is computed on 100 uniformly distributed examples owing to their cost and usage limit

limits: F1 likely overestimates performance: gold '2 apples' scores the same for predictions '2' and 'apples'.
Only one linear algebra dataset, no natural language; theorem proving not covered.
Codex and GPT-3 evaluated on only 100 examples per task, so their numbers are noisy and not comparable to full-test fine-tuned scores.
No training hyperparameters, seeds or compute reported.
OOD defined by random assignment of datasets within a task, so OOD difficulty varies by which datasets land there; tasks with one dataset have no OOD score.
Codex training data is unknown, so contamination with LILA source datasets cannot be ruled out.
Tables 7-9 show identical generated programs across unrelated examples, a probable extraction/typesetting error in the paper.

terms.definition: evaluation set of whole datasets per task held out from training, testing the same skill from independently collected data
evaluation set with linguistic perturbations of questions (9 templates) via crowd-sourcing

Text cites T5-3B 30.1% to 37.6% but Table 5 compares Neo vs Multi with different numbers.
Tables 7-9 generated-program cells repeat the same unrelated sympy snippet (probable PDF/paper error).
Table 15 labels two tasks 'TASK 8' (number theory, linear algebra) and PDF text columns are flattened so IID/OOD membership of datasets in Tables 15-18 is not recoverable from the text.
